clinicalPearls: WHO grade 1 glioneuronal tumour of infancy, typically presenting in the first two years of life as a large supratentorial (usually frontoparietal) mass with a deep cyst and a solid superficial cortical/leptomeningeal-based enhancing nodule attached to the dura.
Common presentation is a rapidly enlarging head circumference, a tense or bulging fontanelle and the setting-sun sign of raised intracranial pressure, sometimes with seizures or a focal deficit.
Despite an alarming size and an occasional primitive small round cell component, the behaviour is overwhelmingly benign.

Histology shows a prominent desmoplastic, reticulin-rich and collagenous stroma with neoplastic astrocytes and a variable ganglionic/neuronal population; desmoplastic infantile astrocytoma (DIA) is the purely astrocytic counterpart on the same spectrum.
Gross total resection is usually curative, with excellent long-term survival even without adjuvant therapy.
A subset harbour MAPK-pathway alterations, including BRAF V600E, which may guide targeted therapy in unresectable or recurrent disease.
Superficial cortical location and dural attachment help distinguish it from deeper infantile embryonal tumours.
Reticulin (silver) staining highlights the characteristic desmoplasia and supports the diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Desmoplastic infantile ganglioglioma and its astrocytic counterpart are rare glioneuronal neoplasms of infancy believed to arise from a subpial bipotential (glial and neuronal) precursor cell within the superficial cortex and leptomeninges. The striking desmoplastic reaction reflects leptomeningeal and mesenchymal involvement with dense reticulin fibre and collagen deposition, and divergent differentiation yields neoplastic astrocytes together with a variable ganglion/neuronal component. A poorly differentiated small round cell (primitive) component may be present but, unlike true embryonal tumours, does not confer aggressive behaviour. A proportion carry activating MAPK-pathway changes, most notably BRAF V600E, driving proliferation, while the tumours characteristically lack the defining molecular hallmarks of other infantile neoplasms.
additionalDifferentials: CNS embryonal tumour (e.g. embryonal tumour with multilayered rosettes)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showing a large cyst with a peripheral cortical-based solid enhancing nodule abutting the dura
CT to assess for calcification and osseous remodelling and for rapid preoperative evaluation
Histopathology with reticulin (silver) staining to demonstrate desmoplasia
Immunohistochemistry (GFAP for astrocytic and synaptophysin/neurofilament/NeuN for neuronal components, with a low proliferation index in differentiated areas)
Molecular testing for BRAF V600E and wider MAPK-pathway alterations
Serial head circumference measurement and developmental assessment
Serum and CSF germ cell tumour markers (alpha-fetoprotein, beta-hCG) when teratoma is considered
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure in an infant: rapidly increasing head circumference, tense fontanelle, vomiting and the setting-sun sign
New or worsening seizures or a focal neurological deficit
Rapid tumour or cyst enlargement with mass effect on serial imaging
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent for this WHO grade 1 tumour, with gross total resection usually curative and prolonged disease-free survival. Incompletely resected or rare atypical cases warrant close surveillance and occasionally adjuvant or BRAF-targeted therapy.
pitfalls: The primitive small-cell component can be mistaken for a malignant embryonal tumour, prompting unnecessary intensive chemoradiotherapy.
The sheer size may lead to an unwarranted assumption of malignancy; grade and behaviour are usually benign.
Failing to recognise the dural and superficial cortical attachment can misdirect the differential toward deep midline tumours.
Overlooking BRAF status may miss a targeted-therapy option in unresectable disease.
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Central Nervous System Tumours
management: Gross total surgical resection is the mainstay and is usually curative for this WHO grade 1 tumour
Perioperative management of raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus, with cerebrospinal fluid diversion or shunting where needed
Seizure control with antiepileptic drugs where seizures are present
Molecular testing for BRAF V600E and wider MAPK-pathway alterations to guide targeted BRAF or MEK inhibitor therapy in unresectable or recurrent disease
Chemotherapy reserved for progressive or incompletely resected tumours
Postoperative surveillance MRI with serial head circumference and developmental monitoring
Manage within a paediatric neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team including neurosurgery, neurology and rehabilitation, escalating for recurrence or incomplete resection
